query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: H2: Partially substituting 1 at% of Co with Hf in the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy will decisively enhance the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy prepared by conventional melting under inert conditions.
generation.intervention: During alloy preparation, replace 1 at% of the Co content with Hf (e.g., modify composition to Cr16Mn16Fe16(Hf0.0625Co15.9375)Ni16P20).
generation.conditions: The alloy must be melted in an inert atmosphere and rapidly cooled (e.g., via melt spinning at ≥3000 K/s) to form an amorphous phase.
generation.structural_mediator: Inclusion of Hf increases lattice distortion (as measured by the δ′ parameter) and lowers the liquidus temperature, effectively suppressing crystal nucleation.
generation.mechanism: Increased lattice distortion from Hf substitution retards atomic rearrangement necessary for nucleation, thereby stabilizing the glassy state and broadening the supercooled liquid region.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Hf-substituted alloy will exhibit a crystallization onset temperature increased by approximately 40–80 K and show improved glass-forming ability compared to the baseline composition.
generation.baseline: The original Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy without any Hf substitution.
generation.boundary: This improvement is limited to rapid cooling conditions; higher Hf levels or deviations from the 1 at% substitution may lead to adverse effects such as reduced ductility or the formation of secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: The 1 at% substitution level is selected based on analogous alloy systems, but its precise impact on ductility and other properties necessitates further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two alloy variants—one baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 and one with 1 at% of Co replaced by Hf. Produce amorphous samples via rapid cooling and compare them by DSC, XRD, and TEM.
measurements: DSC for determining crystallization onset temperatures
XRD for phase analysis and peak broadening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf‐substituted alloy does not show a consistent improvement (e.g., a shift of at least 40 K in onset temperature) and if any undesirable second phases appear, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This has led to the development of high-entropy metallic glasses (HEMGs), where the high mixing entropy combined with an amorphous structure yields materials with enhanced glass-forming ability (GFA) and mechanical stability [,,]. In particular, the addition of phosphorus has been shown to significantly support amorphization processes, thereby promoting the formation of stable metallic glass structures [,].

Its inclusion in Ni-Fe-Cu-P-Si-B alloys also enables the development of extremely soft magnetic materials, broadening the potential applications of these alloys []. Furthermore, recent findings on NiNbP bulk metallic glasses highlight how phosphorus additions enhance glass-forming ability and increase hardness, albeit at the cost of some ductility []. Inspired by these results, this study explores the microstructure, mechanical behavior, and phase stability of phosphorus-containing alloys to better understand and utilize their unique properties. The combination of high configurational entropy and phosphorus enrichment in these alloys suggests their potential for applications in demanding environments that require enhanced wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties position them as promising candidates for use in the aerospace, automotive, and tooling industries, as well as in advanced coating technologies and high-performance structural components. What sets this study apart is the focus on how varying cooling rates, combined with phosphorus addition, influence not only amorphization but also the resulting phase transformations and their potentia

In this paper, two new high entropy bulk metallic glasses (HE-BMGs) have been successfully fabricated using copper mold casting method, namely Ti20Hf20Cu20Ni20Be20 with a critical diameter of 2 mm and Ti16.7Zr16.7Nb16.7Cu16.7Ni16.7Be16.7 with a critical diameter of 1.5 mm. These two HE-BMGs exhibit high fracture strength over 2300 MPa. The glass forming ability and atomic size distribution characteristics of the HE-BMGs are discussed, and it is found that atomic radius spans over a wide range in HE-BMGs. Moreover, we propose a new parameter δ′ to assess the degree of lattice distortion in high entropy alloys (HEAs). It emphasizes the difference between atoms with adjacent atomic size, and it is closely related to phase selection in HEAs. When δ′ is relatively small (δ′ < 2.2), FCC solid solution formed; when 2.2 < δ′ < 2.9, FCC + BCC phases formed; when 2.9 < δ′ < 4.9, BCC phase formed; while δ′ > 4.9, amorphous phase would be formed. papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.approach: The study employed thermal analyses under varied cooling rates (e.g., slow cooling on a copper plate at 52 K/s, rapid cooling after an electric arc pulse at 3018 K/s, and melt-spinning) combined with phase diagram evaluations to investigate the solidification and crystallization behavior.
papers.findings: The findings indicate that the addition of phosphorus broadens the solidification temperature range, significantly reduces the solidification temperatures (e.g., from ~1478 K for the base Cantor alloy to lower ranges in the phosphorus-containing alloy), and promotes the formation of an amorphous phase when cooled rapidly. Specific phase transitions (e.g., at 1291 K, 1206 K, 977 K, 960 K) were noted depending on cooling conditions.
papers.mechanism: Phosphorus is proposed to modify crystallization pathways by promoting the formation of phosphide-rich and eutectic phases, which in turn suppresses conventional crystallization. This alteration in phase formation helps to lower the liquidus temperature and expand the window for amorphization under rapid cooling.

established: Phosphorus addition enhances glass-forming ability (GFA) by broadening the solidification temperature range.
High cooling rates (using techniques such as melt-spinning or electric arc pulsing) are critical to achieving an amorphous structure in these alloys.
Phosphorus influences phase stability by promoting the formation of phosphide-rich or eutectic phases, thereby modifying the crystallization pathway.
The combination of high configurational entropy and phosphorus enrichment can lead to improved thermal stability and amorphization.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying cooling rates (slow cooling vs. rapid cooling) during solidification of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
approaches_tried.outcome: Rapid cooling resulted in a simpler phase composition (or an amorphous phase) whereas slower cooling led to a mixture of multiple crystalline phases; phosphorus was seen to enhance GFA when combined with rapid thermal quenching.

approaches_tried.approach: Manipulating alloy composition by introducing phosphorus into a high-entropy system.
approaches_tried.outcome: Phosphorus addition resulted in a marked reduction in solidification temperatures and a widened temperature range, which is conducive to amorphization.

mechanisms: Phosphorus promotes the formation of phosphide and eutectic phases which lower the liquidus temperature.
Enhanced undercooling due to phosphorus addition suppresses nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
Modified crystallization pathways that favor amorphization rather than multiple crystalline phase formation.
disagreements: While phosphorus addition enhances GFA and thermal stability, there is concern over potential trade-offs such as reduced ductility or adverse effects on mechanical properties.

The precise mechanism—whether the improvement stems solely from phosphide formation or from a more complex interplay between thermodynamic parameters (e.g., undercooling, liquidus temperature depression) and high mixing entropy—is not fully agreed upon.
open_questions: What is the optimal single intervention that can consistently improve both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys?
How does phosphorus interact with other alloying elements specifically at different cooling rates to influence microstructure and thermal behavior?
What are the limits to the beneficial effects of phosphorus addition with respect to mechanical properties such as toughness and ductility?
Can a targeted compositional adjustment (beyond simply adding phosphorus) further optimize the balance between amorphization and thermal stability?
opportunities: Investigate the effect of a precise, single compositional intervention—such as a controlled adjustment in phosphorus content or a micro-alloying addition that further lowers the liquidus temperature—to improve both GFA and thermal stability.
Combine phosphorus addition with fine-tuning of cooling protocols to identify the optimum processing window.

Use advanced characterization methods integrated with machine learning predictive modeling to explore the complex interplay between phosphorus, high mixing entropy, and cooling kinetics in order to design improved high-entropy metallic glasses.
Explore synergistic interventions that adjust lattice distortion (e.g., similar element substitution) concurrently with phosphorus addition to further stabilize the amorphous state.

directions.direction: Micro‐alloying addition of a minor element that is dissimilar in atomic size (e.g., a rare‐earth element such as Gd) to increase atomic size mismatch, liquid viscosity, and undercooling.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the crystallization kinetics and can broaden the glass‐forming window. The supporting evidence indicates that micro‐alloying (e.g., with elements having large atomic radii differences) can significantly alter the nucleation behavior. It is feasible with melt‐spinning and can be falsified by comparing DSC and structural measurements.

directions.direction: Similar element substitution (for instance, substituting a small fraction of a transition metal with Hf) to adjust the lattice distortion parameter δ′ and lower the liquidus temperature.
directions.assessment: This intervention modifies the inherent thermodynamics by increasing lattice distortion, which is known to suppress crystal nucleation. The literature supports that lowering the liquidus temperature can improve glass‐forming ability and thermal stability. It is feasible with conventional alloying techniques and can be directly compared with a baseline alloy.

directions.direction: A controlled post‐solidification thermal annealing (sub‐Tg treatment) to relax the amorphous structure, reduce internal stresses, and improve thermal stability.
directions.assessment: This thermal intervention does not alter the composition but acts on the structure by allowing for relaxation. Evidence suggests that proper annealing near (but below) Tg can increase crystallization onset temperature. It is a practical, scalable method for amorphous alloys and offers clear, falsifiable DSC markers.

directions.direction: Minor addition of a nonmetal element (e.g., boron) to further enhance atomic size mismatch and disrupt short‐range ordering, thereby suppressing crystallization.
directions.assessment: Based on earlier evidence from bulk metallic glasses, adding a small amount of boron is known to improve glass formation by increasing heterogeneity in atomic radii. The intervention is chemically straightforward and can be tested by standard thermal and structural analyses. Its success is contingent upon maintaining boron at a low enough level to avoid forming unwanted boride phases.
